title: Thailand watches deadly tick-borne virus after six SFTS cases

analysis.time: Thailand first confirmed an SFTS case in 2019. The latest cases reported in June 2025 brought the number of identified cases cited by Thai health authorities to six. The publication date is September 13, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Cases were reported in Bangkok, Phetchabun, Nakhon Pathom, and Chachoengsao. The affected population includes people who have close contact with animals that may carry ticks, particularly dogs.
analysis.event: Health authorities are monitoring SFTS, a tick-borne virus that can cause high fever, low platelets, organ failure, and death, after six cases were reported in Thailand. The Department of Disease Control is asking health authorities to strengthen surveillance and follow developments involving SFTS.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Reported fatality rates in affected countries range from 10% to 30%. The virus can begin with sudden high fever, vomiting, and diarrhoea before progressing to thrombocytopenia, liver inflammation, shock, and multiple-organ failure.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Thai authorities are continuing to monitor the situation while urging greater awareness among health workers and the public, particularly where people have close contact with animals that may carry ticks. The department said Thailand has several factors that could allow further infections, including environments suitable for ticks, close contact with pets that may carry ticks, the importation of animals that could harbour ticks, and travel to areas where SFTS is circulating.

analysis.brief_en: Thailand is closely monitoring the Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) virus, which is transmitted by ticks and can lead to high fever, low platelet counts, organ failure, and death. As of June 2025, six confirmed cases have been reported, with locations in Bangkok, Phetchabun, Nakhon Pathom, and Chachoengsao. The Department of Disease Control has urged health authorities to enhance surveillance and awareness, especially among those with close contact with animals that may carry ticks. The virus has been linked to Rhipicephalus sanguineus, the brown dog tick, and has been found in ticks collected from dogs and the environment associated with two fatal human infections. Thai health officials have previously identified the tick species in national parks but have not confirmed its permanent establishment in the country. The reported fatality rates range from 10% to 30% in affected countries, highlighting the severity of the disease. Authorities are emphasizing the importance of considering SFTS in patients with fever and low platelet counts, particularly when there is a history of tick exposure.
analysis.summary_en: Thailand is closely monitoring the Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) virus, which is transmitted by ticks and can lead to high fever, low platelet counts, organ failure, and death. As of June 2025, six confirmed cases have been reported, with locations in Bangkok, Phetchabun, Nakhon Pathom, and Chachoengsao. The virus has been linked to Rhipicephalus sanguineus, the brown dog tick, and has been found in ticks collected from dogs and the environment associated with two fatal human infections. title: New Tick-Borne Virus May Explain Mysterious Cases of Severe Illness - SciTechDaily

analysis.time: Close Menu Facebook X (Twitter) Instagram Biology Chemistry Earth Health Physics Science Space Technology Facebook X (Twitter) Pinterest YouTube RSS Home»Health»New Tick-Borne Virus May Explain Mysterious Cases of Severe Illness Health New Tick-Borne Virus May Explain Mysterious Cases of Severe Illness By Mary Van Beusekom, University of MinnesotaSeptember 12, 2026No Comments4 Mins Read Facebook Twitter Pinterest Telegram LinkedIn WhatsApp Email Reddit Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Telegram Email Reddit Ticks are small blood-feeding arachnids that can carry a wide range of viruses, bacteria, and parasites.
analysis.location_and_population: China, specifically areas where tick-borne viruses circulate.
analysis.event: A newly identified tick-borne virus, Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), may explain unexplained cases of severe tick-related illness, particularly those resembling hemorrhagic fever, despite negative tests for the expected virus, Dabie bandavirus (DBV).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among 3,163 patients tested, 10.4% showed evidence of ALTNV infection. Among patients who tested negative for DBV, 15.1% tested positive for ALTNV. The disease has a reported fatality rate of 10% to 30%, and the World Health Organization lists DBV as a priority for research. The virus was also found in 1.3% of 47,428 ticks collected across 15 Chinese provinces.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Researchers identified ALTNV and determined that it can reproduce in the laboratory. The virus was able to replicate in several types of cells. The cocirculation of ALTNV and DBV in the same areas, coupled with their shared tick vector, underscores the need for improved differential diagnosis between infections with these viruses in regions where SFTS is endemic.

analysis.brief_en: Researchers in China have identified a new tick-borne virus, Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), which may explain unexplained cases of severe tick-related illness, particularly those resembling hemorrhagic fever, despite negative tests for the expected virus, Dabie bandavirus (DBV). Among 3,163 patients tested, 10.4% showed evidence of ALTNV infection, and 15.1% of patients who tested negative for DBV tested positive for ALTNV. The virus was found in 1.3% of 47,428 ticks collected across 15 Chinese provinces, highlighting the need for improved differential diagnosis in affected regions.
analysis.summary_en: Researchers in China have identified a new tick-borne virus, Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), which may explain unexplained cases of severe tick-related illness, particularly those resembling hemorrhagic fever, despite negative tests for the expected virus, Dabie bandavirus (DBV). Among 3,163 patients tested, 10.4% showed evidence of ALTNV infection, and 15.1% of patients who tested negative for DBV tested positive for ALTNV. The virus was found in 1.3% of 47,428 ticks collected across 15 Chinese provinces, highlighting the need for improved differential diagnosis in affected regions.

title: New Tick Virus Found in China

analysis.time: The study was published on September 16, 2026. The event date is not explicitly stated, but the research was conducted in areas where tick-borne viruses are common, with testing of 3,163 patients and 47,428 ticks from 15 Chinese provinces.
analysis.location_and_population: China, specifically 15 provinces where ticks are common. The affected population includes patients who had tick bites and were treated at hospitals in these regions.
analysis.event: Scientists in China identified a new tick-borne virus, named Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), which can cause fever, fatigue, and digestive problems. The discovery was reported in the New England Journal of Medicine by researchers at the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among 3,163 patients examined, 10.4% showed evidence of ALTNV infection. Of those who tested negative for Dabie bandavirus (DBV), 15.1% were found to have ALTNV. The virus was detected in about 1.3% of ticks tested, with the highest rate in Asian longhorned ticks. The study does not confirm the virus's severity or risk to all populations, but it suggests that coinfections with ALTNV and DBV may lead to more severe outcomes, with 18.4% mortality in the coinfected group.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is ongoing, with further research needed to determine the virus's prevalence, severity, and transmission patterns in humans. The researchers have confirmed the virus's ability to reproduce in cells and its presence in ticks, but its full impact and risks remain under investigation. The findings are based on a combination of patient testing, virus isolation, genetic analysis, and tick surveys, making the case for ALTNV as a genuine tick-borne virus convincing, though more data is required.

analysis.brief_en: Scientists in China have identified a new tick-borne virus, named Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), which can cause fever, fatigue, and digestive problems. The discovery, reported in the New England Journal of Medicine, was made by researchers at the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing. Among 3,163 patients examined, 10.4% showed evidence of ALTNV infection, with 15.1% of those who tested negative for Dabie bandavirus (DBV) being found to have ALTNV. The virus was detected in about 1.3% of ticks tested, with the highest rate in Asian longhorned ticks. While the study suggests that coinfections with ALTNV and DBV may lead to more severe outcomes, it does not confirm the virus's full risk or prevalence. Further research is needed to understand its impact on human health and its role in tick-borne disease transmission. The findings highlight the importance of surveillance and better diagnostic tools to distinguish between similar infections.

title: New Tick-Borne Virus Discovered in China Traced to Hundreds of Fever Cases

analysis.time: Open menu NTD Television U.S.ChinaWorldPoliticsHealthBusinessEntertainmentSports More ●LIVE search EN▼ NTD Television NewsChina News New Tick-Borne Virus Discovered in China Traced to Hundreds of Fever Cases Chinese researchers, working with U.S.
analysis.location_and_population: China, specifically areas where tick-borne diseases are common.
analysis.event: A new tick-borne virus, Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), has been identified and linked to hundreds of previously unexplained fever cases in China. The virus is associated with a flu-like illness and co-infection with Dabie bandavirus (DBV) can lead to more serious illness.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 10.4 percent of 3,163 patients tested positive for ALTNV, with 15.1 percent of those who tested negative for DBV being positive for ALTNV. Among 38 patients co-infected with ALTNV and DBV, 18.4 percent died. The virus is detected in 1.29 percent of Asian longhorned ticks, with the highest detection rate in Haemaphysalis longicornis. The virus is associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, low platelet counts, and elevated liver enzymes.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The discovery was published in The New England Journal of Medicine. The researchers recommend better testing to distinguish between ALTNV and DBV infections. The USDA has no evidence that ALTNV is circulating in U.S. tick populations or causing human infections in the United States.

analysis.brief_en: Chinese researchers, working with U.S. collaborators, have identified a new tick-borne virus, Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), linked to hundreds of unexplained fever cases in China. The virus is associated with flu-like symptoms and co-infection with Dabie bandavirus (DBV) can lead to more severe illness. Among 38 co-infected patients, 18.4 percent died. The virus is detected in 1.29 percent of Asian longhorned ticks, with the highest detection rate in Haemaphysalis longicornis. The researchers recommend better testing to distinguish between ALTNV and DBV infections.
analysis.summary_en: Chinese researchers, working with U.S. collaborators, have identified a new tick-borne virus, Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), linked to hundreds of unexplained fever cases in China.
